identification.summary: AhnLab classifies cyberattacks against Korean companies and organizations that use Shadow Force and Wgdrop malware as Operation Shadow Force, a name taken from the Shadow Force malware the group mainly used [S1]. AhnLab's first confirmed attack was in March 2013, with activity likely before 2012 based on malware creation dates, and in 2020 AhnLab had not confirmed any link to a known group [S1]. A 2023 AhnLab report says the group has targeted South Korean organizations since 2013, mainly Windows servers [S2][S4]. The 2025 AhnLab/NCSC joint report tracks the successor activity as TA-ShadowCricket, first tracked as Larva-24013 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: March 2013 (first confirmed attack); likely active before 2012 [S1]. Virus Bulletin abstract says active since 2014 mainly in South Korea [S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is known for this cluster. Dates of first activity differ across AhnLab documents (2012/2013 in the 2020 report [S1]; 2014 in the VB2023 abstract [S3]); not reconciled. The VB2023 abstract describes the group as 'reportedly' Chinese-speaking [S3].

attribution.confidence: Low. AhnLab stated in 2020 that it had not confirmed whether the attacker is associated with a known group [S1]. The Virus Bulletin 2023 abstract describes the group only as reportedly Chinese-speaking [S3]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: AhnLab malware analysis, certificate analysis and code-lineage work [S1][S3][S5].

regions: Asia-Pacific, including Maggie-infected MS-SQL servers with APAC concentration (Maggie link to Shadow Force is a hypothesis, not confirmed) [S3][S6]
targeting.notes: Sources describe targets as Korean companies and organizations and Windows servers, not specific industry sectors [S1][S2]. Sector list left empty.

capabilities.summary: Core malware is Shadow Force and Wgdrop [S1]. AhnLab's operation timeline lists an MS-SQL server intrusion by an unknown method, Htran (aio.exe) to download further malware, and a PE modifier (iatinfect.exe) that patches EXE files [S2][S4]. Malware has been signed with forged or stolen digital certificates of Korean companies [S1][S3]. After 2020 older backdoors were used less, with Viticdoor appearing and cryptocurrency miners installed alongside since December 2021 [S2][S4]. The actor has reused the same file names and similar tools since 2014, which aids detection [S2]. The 2025 joint report describes the successor cluster using IRC bots and backdoors against exposed Windows remote access and poorly managed MS-SQL servers [S5].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed actor tracked by AhnLab as Operation Shadow Force, later TA-ShadowCricket; reportedly Chinese-speaking [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Shadow Force, Wgdrop, Viticdoor, Htran, iatinfect.exe PE patcher, cryptocurrency miners, IRC bots [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised MS-SQL and Windows servers; forged or stolen Korean-company code-signing certificates [S1][S3]. IRC command infrastructure for TA-ShadowCricket [S5].
diamond.victim: Korean companies and organizations, mainly Windows servers [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed, poorly managed MS-SQL and Windows remote access services; trust in code-signed binaries [S1][S5].

gaps: Sponsor, motive and objective are not established in any source gathered; AhnLab stated no link to a known group was confirmed [S1].
Initial access vector is described as unknown (MS-SQL intrusion by unknown method) [S2][S4].

I could not open the AhnLab primary reports, the VB2023 paper/slides or the ASEC TA-ShadowCricket post (fetch failed); statements rely on search-result summaries and should be validated against the originals.

Search summaries disagreed on whether TA-ShadowCricket is the same actor as Shadow Force; the AhnLab/NCSC-focused result states Larva-24013 was linked to Shadow Force and reclassified [S5]. Confirm in the primary report.
Secondary coverage (not cited) calls TA-ShadowCricket China-linked and reports over 2,000 compromised systems; not verified against AhnLab text.
Whether the Maggie backdoor belongs to this group is a hypothesis raised by AhnLab, not a confirmed link [S3][S6].
Wgdrop details were not found beyond its naming as a defining malware family [S1].
Sector-level targeting is not documented in sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-exposed MS-SQL and Windows remote-access servers are key terrain, particularly in South Korea and the wider Asia-Pacific [S1][S5]. STEP 2: Weakly managed database servers and code-signing trust are exploitable seams [S1][S5]. STEP 3: Template is server intrusion, Htran-assisted tool download, PE patching for persistence, then backdoor or IRC bot, with miners as monetization [S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic compromise of Korean and APAC Windows servers, which the available sources do not tie to a specific sector. MDCOA is use of a compromised, trusted-signed server as a staging node against allied networks in the theater; this is judgment and not shown in sources. Candidate indicators: iatinfect.exe or aio.exe on database servers, unexpected extended-stored-procedure DLLs on MS-SQL, IRC traffic from servers, and binaries signed with certificates later reported as leaked [S2][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track AhnLab and Korean NCSC reporting on this cluster for ROK-hosted infrastructure that coalition networks may touch [S5]. (2) Authorities: activity is on Korean and third-country servers, so hunt or response actions off DoD networks need host-nation and legal coordination. (3) Mission assurance: harden and inventory any internet-exposed MS-SQL and RDP-type services supporting mission systems; miner activity is an early sign of server compromise [S2][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with ROK counterparts and DC3 as appropriate; avoid assuming state sponsorship given low-confidence attribution [S1].
